title: Netsuke of Three Rats

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Russell Sage, 1910

altText: A tiny carved ivory sculpture of three rats, their forms close together, with smooth, pale, rounded surfaces.

context: A netsuke by an artist named Nagahisa, carved from ivory in Japan in the first half of the 19th century. Netsuke were small toggles used to hang pouches from the sash of a kimono. The rat is the first animal in the twelve-animal zodiac used in Japan.

descriptions.k: Look at three little rats made from ivory. They are very small. They are carved so well that you can almost feel their smooth backs. How might they be sitting together? What would they say to each other?
descriptions.g12: Three rats are carved from pale ivory. This sculpture is called a netsuke, and it is small enough to hold in your hand. People in Japan used netsuke like a button to hang a pouch from a belt. Look at how the rats fit together. Which parts are smooth, and which parts have tiny details?
descriptions.g35: Kimono had no pockets, so people in Japan hung pouches from their sashes using a cord and a small toggle called a netsuke. This netsuke shows three rats carved from ivory by an artist named Nagahisa. Because it was worn and handled, the surface had to be smooth and the shape compact. Look at how the rats are grouped. Why might an artist choose rats, and how did the artist fit three animals into one tiny object?
descriptions.g68: Nagahisa carved this netsuke in the early 1800s. Netsuke solved a practical problem: kimono lack pockets, so a toggle kept a pouch from slipping from the sash. Because they were handled constantly, makers designed them without sharp points and often with a cord hole hidden in the design. Rats are the first animal of the zodiac and appear in many folk stories. How does the sculptor group three animals into a single compact form? Why would a small object be worth such skill?
descriptions.g910: Netsuke are a case where craft, function, and wit meet. This ivory sculpture by Nagahisa, from the first half of the 19th century, packs three rats into a compact group that could be worn and handled daily. Its success depends on balancing volume, surface detail, and the need to avoid fragile projections. Rats carry varied associations in Japanese culture, including cleverness and prosperity, though any one reading depends on context. Consider how the small scale invites close, tactile looking rather than distant display.
descriptions.g1112: Nagahisa's netsuke shows how an everyday fastener became a sophisticated sculptural genre in Edo-period Japan. The work must function as a toggle, so its design negotiates compactness, durability, and a cord path while still delivering naturalistic observation and humor. Rats in Japan could suggest wealth or cleverness depending on context. Ivory also raises present-day questions, because the material is now heavily regulated, and museums consider how to present historical works made from it. How do function, subject, and material shape meaning here?

teacherNote.context: A small ivory netsuke by Nagahisa, first half of the 19th century. Netsuke served as toggles for pouches hung from the sash of a kimono, which has no pockets.
directions: Have students sketch the netsuke from imagined front, back, and top views to practice sculptural thinking.
Ask students to design a toggle for something they carry and explain the function of each part.
Discuss historic ivory objects and why present-day laws restrict ivory trade.
